summary: Calcium acetate is an oral phosphate binder used to reduce serum phosphorus in patients with end-stage renal disease, typically on dialysis. Taken with meals, the calcium combines with dietary phosphate to form an insoluble complex that is eliminated in the stool. It is one of the more efficient calcium-based binders per unit of elemental calcium. The principal hazard is hypercalcemia, so serum calcium must be monitored, the calcium-phosphate product kept below 55 mg2/dL2, and concurrent calcium supplements/vitamin D analogues used cautiously. It can reduce absorption of co-administered tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and other drugs, which should be separated in time.
indications: Reduction of serum phosphorus (control of hyperphosphatemia) in patients with end-stage renal disease

dosage.n: Most patients require 3-4 doses per day with meals

moa: Calcium acetate dissociates in the gastrointestinal tract to release calcium ions, which combine with dietary phosphate to form insoluble calcium phosphate. This complex is not absorbed and is excreted in the feces, thereby decreasing the amount of phosphate available for systemic absorption and lowering serum phosphorus concentration. Relative to other calcium salts, calcium acetate binds more phosphate per unit of elemental calcium and is less pH-dependent, reducing the calcium load needed for a given phosphate-binding effect.

relative: Concurrent vitamin D therapy or calcium supplements (additive hypercalcemia risk)
Adynamic bone disease or low bone turnover
monitor: Serum calcium (twice weekly during initial dosing and titration)

preg: Pregnancy Category C. There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Calcium acetate is not expected to harm the fetus when maternal calcium levels are appropriately monitored and maintained.
lact: Calcium acetate is considered compatible with breastfeeding provided maternal serum calcium is appropriately monitored; the normal calcium content of milk is not expected to be significantly altered.
renal: Calcium acetate is specifically indicated for hyperphosphatemia of end-stage renal disease, including dialysis patients; no separate renal dose adjustment is defined, but the dose is titrated to serum phosphorus while avoiding hypercalcemia.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is provided for hepatic impairment.

major: Digoxin - hypercalcemia from calcium therapy can potentiate digoxin toxicity
moderate: Tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) - calcium reduces absorption ~50%; separate dosing
Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) - reduced absorption; separate dosing
Vitamin D analogues and calcium supplements - additive risk of hypercalcemia
minor: Levothyroxine and bisphosphonates - reduced absorption if taken together
interactions.food: Must be taken WITH meals to bind dietary phosphate; this is essential to its action.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum calcium; monitor calcium and the calcium-phosphorus product.

emergency: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (confusion, stupor, coma, cardiac arrhythmia)

missed: If you miss a dose with a meal, take it as soon as you remember if you are still eating or shortly after; otherwise skip it and take the next dose with your next meal. Do not double up.
overdose: Excessive administration causes hypercalcemia, which may present with constipation, nausea, vomiting, weakness, confusion, and in severe cases stupor, coma, or cardiac arrhythmia. Management includes stopping the drug, reducing calcium and vitamin D intake, hydration, and dialysis with a low-calcium dialysate; severe hypercalcemia is treated as a medical emergency.
